title: Will a Heart That Lives on Hopes Never Sober Up?
intro: Jarir taunts his rival al-Akhtal after al-Jahhaf’s raid on Taghlib at al-Bishr. Ibn Habib connects the taunt with al-Akhtal’s own lament for his people. After an opening among deserted dwellings, the stars of a lover’s sleepless night give way to the lights of an approaching army. Jarir lays the dead at his rival’s door and ends by naming the Umayyad family whose protection keeps the survivors alive.

translation: Will a heart that lives on hopes really never sober up,
though grey shows on cheek and chin?
1.sharh: Grey is showing at the sides of his face and under his chin. The heart goes on living on promises, like someone who has still to sober up.

translation: If only those who left Dhu al-Ghada
had stayed, and some of the others had moved on.
2.sharh: He would exchange some of the people who stayed for the ones who went away. That impossible bargain gives a particular address to his longing.

translation: One day they humour love without any real desire,
another you see a ghoul among them changing shape.
3.sharh: One day their words keep pace with his desires. The next day their behaviour is as bewildering as the shifting shapes of the ghoul in travellers’ tales.

translation: Valley whose people have gone away,
doves and little warblers live in their dwellings now.
4.sharh: He can still address the valley. The settlement even has inhabitants, but its small bird voices make the absence of human ones audible.

translation: Let others watch Orion or spend a long night.
Mine at al-Majaza is longer.
5.sharh: Watching the stars travel measures the hours without a clock. He claims a still longer night at a named stopping place on the desert road.

translation: Dawbal wept. May God never dry his tears.
It is humiliation that makes Dawbal weep.
6.sharh: The childhood nickname cuts the adult poet down to size. Jarir recasts his rival’s grief for his people as tears of humiliation, part of the taunt he is building.

translation: You lost heart, son of the woman with the cord, when
war’s fangs and heavy breast closed upon you.
7.sharh: The slur plays on a word for a heavy cord, understood by al-Baghdadi as a Christian girdle. War bites like a beast, then pins its victim under its chest.

translation: When you goaded al-Jahhaf that day,
you counted on delay. He came to water sooner.
8.sharh: He says the challenge assumed there would be time to spare. An army arriving unexpectedly is pictured as riders reaching their water before the reckoning allowed.

translation: A night advanced towards you, its stars like lamps
with tightly twisted wicks.
9.sharh: Ibn Habib reads the moving night as the mass of the army and the stars as the glint of weapons. Lamps and their twisted wicks bring that vast sky within reach.

translation: By the time dawn broke they could make out
squadrons led by a white-socked bay.
10.sharh: Daylight resolves the dark mass into squadrons. The conspicuous bay with white markings stands for al-Jahhaf at their head in Ibn Habib’s commentary.

translation: At the onslaught of Qays your women cast out
their children, some full-term and some before their time.
11.sharh: The raid is measured by what it does to women in labour. Jarir deliberately sets babies born at term beside those delivered too soon, confronting his rival with both.

translation: A woman put to death in captivity, a child cut out
at her feet, and another wife crying aloud.
12.sharh: One captive lies dead with a child cut from the womb at her feet. Beside this still picture he places the voice of a living woman wailing.

translation: Al-Jahhaf killed the children of women
whom Ibn Khallas and Azhal drive before them.
13.sharh: The recording makes the captives mothers bereaved of children. Ibn Habib’s reading makes them widows. Either way the naming of the two men driving them adds the indignity of captivity to bereavement.

translation: The bereaved mother whose husband was struck down tells you,
“Abu Malik, there is no courting among these women.”
14.sharh: The bereaved woman addresses al-Akhtal by his familiar name. The travelling women of a conventional love prelude now travel as captives, with no occasion for flirtation.

translation: You urged them on against the people you abandoned,
where Rudayni spears drink and drink again.
15.sharh: The accuser puts the instigator safely away from the scene. Two verbs from watering a herd give the spears a first drink of blood and a return draught.

translation: The eagle of death wheels above them.
Horses with tangled forelocks make their bits ring.
16.sharh: Ibn Habib sees a battle standard in the wheeling eagle. Below it the dishevelled horses lend the scene a sound, the clattering metal of the bits.

translation: At the Tigris, if they turn back, Qays stands behind them
in ranks. If they make for the ford, they bog down.
17.sharh: The two conditional clauses map the trap. One exit leads into ranks of fighting men and the other into river mud.

translation: The blood of the dead kept flowing
in the Tigris, till the Tigris water itself ran red.
18.sharh: The ford has just offered a possible way out. Now the blood reaches the water, and the second mention of the Tigris makes the river itself bear the mark of the battle.

translation: Unless you hold to a pledge of protection from Quraysh,
there is no counting on the swords of Qays.
19.sharh: The guarantee of Quraysh is the one thing he concedes might stop pursuit. That concession prepares the final appeal to the authority of the Marwanids.

translation: We have the advantage in this world, though your nose bites dust,
and on Judgement Day we rank above you too.
20.sharh: The defeated man’s nose is rubbed in the dust. Jarir extends a tribal boast into the afterlife, exploiting the difference of religion between himself and the Christian al-Akhtal.

translation: On the day of al-Rahub our swords split
shoulders that could no longer bear a sword strap.
21.sharh: A shoulder once supported the fighting man’s sword belt. The wound is measured by the small, familiar piece of equipment it can no longer hold.

translation: The sons of Marwan spared your blood from them.
Who stands higher or has greater merit than Marwan’s sons?
22.sharh: The Marwanid rulers receive the closing compliment. It doubles as a final insult to the rival whose people, on Jarir’s account, owe their lives to someone else’s protection.

1.1.1.meaning: “In all earnest?”, a challenge to the speaker’s own heart.

1.1.5.head: مُعَلَّل
1.1.5.meaning: Kept going on promises or hopes.

1.2.5.head: عِذار
1.2.5.meaning: Hair along the cheek in front of the ear.

1.2.6.head: مِسحَل
1.2.6.meaning: The part beneath the chin, as Ibn Habib explains it.

2.1.4.head: ظاعِن
2.1.4.meaning: One who breaks camp and departs.

2.1.5-6.head: ذو الغَضا
2.1.5-6.meaning: Dhu al-Ghada, a place named for a tree of sandy country.

3.1.2.head: جارى
3.1.2.meaning: Went along with another’s professions of love.

3.2.5.head: تَغَوَّلَ
3.2.5.meaning: Changed shape, as a ghoul was believed to do.

4.2.2.head: مَغنىً
4.2.2.meaning: An inhabited dwelling or settlement, recalled after its people depart.

4.2.4.head: دُخَّل
4.2.4.meaning: Small birds, described by Ibn Habib as smaller than sparrows.

5.1.3.head: الجَوزاء
5.1.3.meaning: Al-Jawza, Orion, watched through the night.

5.2.3.head: المَجازَة
5.2.3.meaning: Al-Majaza, on the Basra road at the edge of the Dahna sands.

6.1.4.head: أَرقَأَ
6.1.4.meaning: Staunched a flow of tears or blood.

7.1.4.head: قَلس
7.1.4.meaning: A stout cord, read here as a Christian girdle. Ibn Habib gives fals, a small coin.

7.2.5.head: كَلكَل
7.2.5.meaning: A beast’s breast, bearing hard on one it has thrown down.

8.1.2.head: الجَحّاف
8.1.2.meaning: Al-Jahhaf ibn Hakim, the Sulami who led the raid on Taghlib.

8.2.4.head: وِرد
8.2.4.meaning: Coming to water, here the army’s arrival.

10.2.1.head: كُردوس
10.2.1.meaning: A troop or squadron gathered in one body.

10.2.3-4.head: وَرد مُحَجَّل
10.2.3-4.meaning: “A white-socked bay”, a reddish horse with white leg markings.

11.2.4.head: مُعجَل
11.2.4.meaning: A child delivered before its full term.

12.1.2.meaning: In captivity, held fast for killing.

12.2.1.head: بَقير
12.2.1.meaning: A child cut from its mother’s womb.

13.1.4.head: وَلَد
13.1.4.meaning: Children. Ibn Habib and al-Baghdadi give “husbands of women”. The reciter and his verse card have “children”.

13.2.2-3.head: اِبن خَلّاس
13.2.2-3.meaning: Ibn Khallas, one of the two men Ibn Habib identifies as Qaysis driving the captives.

13.2.5.head: عَزهَل
13.2.5.meaning: Azhal, the other Qaysi driving the captives.

14.2.6.head: مَغزَل
14.2.6.meaning: An occasion for courtship or love play.

15.2.2.head: رُدَينِيَّة
15.2.2.meaning: Rudayni, a spear traditionally associated with Rudayna.

15.2.4.head: نَهِلَ
15.2.4.meaning: Drank a first draught. The other verb in the half describes a second drink.

16.1.1-2.head: عُقاب المَنايا
16.1.1-2.meaning: “Death’s eagle”, the battle standard in Ibn Habib’s reading.

16.2.3.head: لِجام
16.2.3.meaning: A bridle and bit, here the clattering metal in the horses’ mouths.

17.2.4.head: مَخاضَة
17.2.4.meaning: A ford, a shallow place for crossing a river.

18.1.4.head: مارَ
18.1.4.meaning: Surged or flowed, here said of the blood.

18.2.5.head: أَشكَل
18.2.5.meaning: Tinged with red, as in the white of a bloodshot eye.

19.1.5.head: ذِمَّة
19.1.5.meaning: A pledge of protection extended to someone.

20.1.6.head: راغِم
20.1.6.meaning: Rubbed in dust, an expression of humiliation.

21.1.4.head: الرَّحوب
21.1.4.meaning: Al-Rahub, the place that gives the battle its name here.

21.2.1.head: عاتِق
21.2.1.meaning: The shoulder between neck and upper arm, where a sword strap rests.

21.2.5.head: مِحمَل
21.2.5.meaning: A strap for slinging a sword from the shoulder.

22.1.2-3.head: بَنو مَروان
22.1.2-3.meaning: Banu Marwan, the ruling Marwanid branch of the Umayyad family.
